newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian railways blame weather for grain delays.
newsitem.headline: Canadian railways blame weather for grain delays.

text.p: Canadian railway officials on Wednesday denied claims that a federal cap on rates was responsible for delayed grain shipments to Pacific ports, and blamed harsher than usual winter weather instead.
"We may be at that (maximum federally mandated) C$34 cap but that's not a factor in the situation we're in right now," Canadian National Railway Co spokesman Jim Feeny said.
"We treat grain very, very seriously and we at CP are doing everything we can to get things back to normal," CP Rail System spokesman Steve Morris said.
Morris blamed the delays on avalanches, record Pacific coast snowfall and temperatures cold enough to affect locomotive operation.

Air brakes on locomotives function less effectively below -25 degrees Celsius because the temperature thins the air so that a 100-unit train hauled by three locomotives at -25 C requires six engines at -40 C, Morris said.

The Canadian Wheat Board and grain and transportation analysts have charged that grain shipments were a lower priority for the railways since they generate less profit than other commodities that do not have a maximum rail rate imposed by law.
The maximum rate to ship grains and oilseed from the farthest point inland in mid-Saskatchewan to either Vancouver or Thunder Bay is C$34.09 a tonne, CN's Feeny said.
"That cap has not influenced our priorities," Feeny said.
But a Wheat Board advisory committee was unconvinced.

"While other commodities seem to have caught up after the weather problems we experienced earlier this winter, grain movement through the West Coast is the worst it has ever been in a non-strike stiuation," CWB adviser Bill Nicholson said.

Forty-three ocean vessels were waiting to load grains and oilseeds at Canada's Pacific ports on Tuesday. Some ships had been berthed as long as 40 days. The Wheat Board said it faces C$15 million in demurrage fines because of the delays since early January.
The Vancouver Port Corporation said two ships were waiting for coal and two for sulfur, the CWB committee said.
About C$285 million worth of wheat and barley may not be able to be sold in the 1996/97 (August/July) crop year because of the delay, the committee added.
CP's Morris acknowledged that coal, potash and sulfur, which do not have rate caps, were moving faster to export ports.

"Those commodities are easier to bring back on stream after the weather delays we had because you can take a 100-car train to one plant or one mine to load and take it to one location on the coast and the train never uncouples," he said.
Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale called a meeting of rail and grain industry leaders for Thursday evening in Calgary to address the shipment problem.

"Locomotive power in the fleet seems to be undersupplied, and those two factors have put the whole system way behind putting the grain through the Rockies," Goodale told reporters in Ottawa, referring to a locomotive shortage and bad weather.
CN has more than 14,000 grain hopper cars and 1,892 locomotives in its fleet. CP has more than 14,300 grain hopper cars and 1,475 locomotives and has leased another 250 locomotives.
Goodale dismissed suggestions that the rate cap may be at fault.

"The problem is that we've had a very difficult winter season with more snow and more cold than usual and at the same time the locomotive power seems to be undersupplied, and those are the factors that put the system way behind," Goodale said.
((Winnipeg bureau 204 947 3548))
